title: Magic vs BELAY: Pricing and Coverage Compared (2026)
summary: Magic charges a fixed $540 a week for a full-time assistant. BELAY quotes each client, anywhere from $30 to $75 an hour. Here's how the two compare.
body_text: 9 min read Quick summary Magic and BELAY are both fully managed services. Each one hires, trains, and replaces your assistant for you. Three things separate them: where the assistants are based, how the pricing works, and whether anyone covers the work when your assistant is away. Magic charges a fixed weekly rate. Full-time is $540 a week for 40 hours and includes Magic 24/7 at no extra cost (part-time is $270 a week for 20 hours). Both plans work out to $13.50 an hour. BELAY quotes each client after a consultation, so the cost varies and you find out yours on the call. BELAY’s site says US-based assistants cost $30 to $75 an hour. If you need an assistant based in the US, choose BELAY. If you don’t, Magic costs less and includes backup coverage. What we found Magic costs less for the same number of hours. At around 1,000 hours a year, Magic runs $14,040. The same hours at the bottom of BELAY’s stated range come to $31,200. Magic includes backup coverage. Full-time plans come with Magic 24/7 , a shared pool that picks up work when your assistant is unavailable. BELAY provides a dedicated assistant and doesn’t list a backup option. Magic pays for its assistants’ AI tools. Every assistant gets access to leading LLMs and training on how to use them, at no extra charge to you. BELAY hires in the US. Magic hires in the Philippines and Latin America. Every Magic assistant works US hours. What you pay Magic’s rate is the same on both plans and doesn’t change by client. Full pricing is on the pricing page. Magic plan Hours a week Price Hourly Full-time, includes Magic 24/7 40 $540/wk $13.50 Part-time 20 $270/wk $13.50 Billing runs every four weeks and there’s no charge until you start working with your assistant. BELAY prices each client individually. Here is what BELAY’s site says a US-based assistant costs: “On average, U.S.-based virtual assistants charge $30 to $75 per hour. That translates to around $1,200 to $3,000 per month for part-time support. Simpler admin tasks like calendar management, email triage, or data entry tend to fall on the lower end. More specialized services like bookkeeping, marketing support, or executive-level assistance land higher.” BELAY, How much does it cost to hire a virtual assistant in the U.S.? That’s a range of more than two times. Where you land depends on scope, hours, and how specialized the work is, and you find out after the consultation. Cost for the same hours Magic’s part-time plan is 20 hours a week, or about 1,040 hours a year. The figures below use BELAY’s own stated rate for the same number of hours. Around 1,040 hours a year Magic BELAY Hourly rate $13.50, fixed on both plans $30 to $75, BELAY’s stated range Cost for the year $14,040 $31,200 to $78,000 The gap is about $17,000 at BELAY’s lowest stated rate and about $64,000 at their highest, depending on the quote you’re given. Client reports suggest a typical BELAY client pays nearer $42 an hour, or around $45,600 a year, though those figures are estimates and BELAY doesn’t confirm them. Magic full-time is 40 hours a week, about 2,080 hours a year, at $28,080. No upfront cost Meet your assistant before you pay anything Talk to your assistant before you commit. You pay nothing until you actually start working with them. Get started with Magic → Side by side Feature Magic BELAY Rate $13.50 an hour , fixed on both plans $30 to $75 an hour by BELAY’s own figures Price $540/wk full-time ($270/wk part-time) Custom quote. Client reports estimate around $3,800/mo. How you get a price On the pricing page Consultation, then a custom quote Talent based in Philippines and Latin America United States, across 48 states Time zone US hours US hours Employment type Managed contractors 1099 contractors Model Dedicated executive assistant , plus a 24/7 shared pool Dedicated one to one Backup coverage Included with full-time, via Magic 24/7 None listed AI tools Paid for by Magic, with training before they start Assistants use AI and automation Acceptance rate Top 0.5% of applicants Top 3% of US applicants Replacement Free, preferences carry over Free rematch under the Right-Fit Guarantee Commitment No long-term contract, cancel anytime Month to month, 30-day notice Backup when your assistant is away Assistants take holidays, get sick, and go on leave. What happens to the work during those days is worth checking before you sign with either service. Every Magic full-time plan includes Magic 24/7 , a shared pool of assistants who pick up tasks when your dedicated assistant is unavailable. You send the request and someone handles it. BELAY provides a dedicated assistant during business hours. Their service list doesn’t include a backup or on-demand option, so you’d need to ask how they cover time off. AI tools Every Magic assistant gets access to leading LLMs and AI tools, plus training on how to use them before they start working with you. Magic pays for the tools. BELAY says its assistants use AI and automation to enhance rather than replace expertise. Their site doesn’t say which tools assistants get or who pays for them, so you’d need to ask on the call. Vetting and training Magic accepts the top 0.5% of applicants. BELAY accepts the top 3% of US applicants. Every Magic assistant goes through training on AI tools before their first task for you. We don’t have information on whether BELAY trains its assistants. Contracts and cancellation Both services run month to month with no long-term contract. BELAY asks for 30 days’ notice to cancel. Magic lets you cancel at any time. The other difference is when you commit. BELAY’s process is a sales call, then an agreement, then a discovery call. BELAY selects your assistant and introduces them at a kickoff call. With Magic you meet your assistant first, and there’s no charge until you start working together. Why choose BELAY If you need an assistant based in the US, choose BELAY. BELAY hires in the US, across 48 states. Magic’s assistants are in the Philippines and Latin America. All of them work US time zones. Why choose Magic If you’re willing to hire outside the US, choose Magic. Lower cost. $13.50 an hour, fixed on both plans. It varies by a significant amount. BELAY’s site says US-based virtual assistants cost $30 to $75 an hour, or $1,200 to $3,000 a month for part-time support. You need to get on a call for a custom quote. Client reports estimate a typical BELAY client pays around $3,800 a month for a little under 90 hours, roughly $42 an hour, though BELAY doesn’t confirm those figures. Where are Magic assistants based? Magic assistants are in the Philippines and Latin America, and all of them work US time zones. BELAY hires in the US, across 48 states. What can a Magic assistant do? Magic assistants cover executive and administrative work across more than a hundred task types, including inbox and calendar management, travel, research, project coordination, bookkeeping support, and personal tasks. See what an executive assistant handles day to day. Magic isn’t built for senior specialist roles like a lead developer or designer. How selective is Magic’s hiring? Magic accepts the top 0.5% of applicants. Every assistant who gets through goes through training on AI tools before their first task. BELAY accepts the top 3% of US applicants. What happens when my assistant is on leave? Every Magic full-time plan includes Magic 24/7 , a shared pool of assistants who pick up tasks when your dedicated assistant is unavailable. BELAY provides a dedicated assistant during business hours and doesn’t list a backup option. Do Magic assistants use AI tools? Yes. Every Magic assistant gets access to leading LLMs and AI tools, plus training on how to use them before they start. Magic pays for the tools. Magic replaces them at no extra cost and your saved preferences carry over, so the new assistant starts with the same context. BELAY offers a free rematch under its Right-Fit Guarantee. Can I cancel anytime? Magic has no long-term contract and you can cancel at any time. BELAY also runs month to month and asks for 30 days’ notice. Which is better, Magic or BELAY? It depends on whether you need someone based in the US. If you do, choose BELAY. If you don’t, Magic costs less for the same hours and includes backup coverage and paid AI access. Adds StockTitan as a preferred source · opens Google Add on Google 07/02/2026 - 09:00 AM NEW YORK CITY, NY / ACCESS Newswire / July 2, 2026 / Emerging Growth Research today issued a flash report on OSR Health, Inc. (NASDAQ: OSRH ), formerly OSR Holdings, reaffirming its Buy-Emerging rating and 12-month price target of $10.00. The flash report highlights OSRH 's newly announced Shareholder Loyalty Program, a novel plan to reward long-term shareholders with Contingent Value Rights ("CVR") rather than pursuing a reverse stock split. The Company's Board has approved the plan, which remains subject to legal counsel's opinion, with a record date targeted for July 31, 2026. Key Highlights From the Flash Report: Shareholder Loyalty Program via Contingent Value Rights: OSRH plans to distribute one non-transferable CVR for every share held as of the expected record date, at no cost to shareholders. As the Company's share price reaches a series of defined milestones over the 12 months following the record date, shareholders who continuously hold their shares automatically receive additional shares of common stock. Tiered, Cumulative Reward Structure: Rewards are delivered in four tiers: at a share price ≥$2.00 sustained for 3 months, a CVR delivers 0.5 additional shares; ≥$3.00 for 6 months delivers 1.0 shares; ≥$4.00 for 9 months delivers 1.5 shares; and ≥$5.00 for 12 months delivers 2.0 shares. A shareholder who remains invested through all four milestones over 12 months would theoretically receive five additional shares per original share, growing their position to six times its original size. An Alternative to a Reverse Split: Emerging Growth Research believes the CVR structure is likely the first time a company has used this mechanism to provide an asymmetric upside incentive for shareholders, and views it as preferable to a reverse stock split. Rather than reducing share count and liquidity in a manner that could give short sellers another opportunity to press the stock lower, the program is designed to reward loyal holders with additional shares while potentially improving trading liquidity and discouraging short selling. Building on the $815 Million BCM Europe Licensing Deal: The loyalty program builds on the strategic strength of OSRH 's $815 million licensing agreement this year with BCM Europe for VXM01. Emerging Growth Research notes that continued execution on the BCM Europe relationship, growth in 4PL, integration of Woori IO's non-invasive glucose monitor into the global wearables market through Big Tech partnerships, and progress in drug candidate development represent substantial sources of potential price upside. Share Price Dynamics and Potential Floor: OSRH shares have experienced volatility over the past year. Emerging Growth Research believes a potential floor may now be forming in the stock if short sellers are brought to heel by the new loyalty program's design. For a copy of the full flash report, please visit: https://emerginggrowth.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/OSRH_Flash-Report_05.05.26.pdf or https://emerginggrowth.com/profile/osrh/ (on the right side of the page as you scroll down) About OSR Health, Inc. Founded in 2020 and headquartered in Bellevue, Washington, and Gyeonggi-do, South Korea, OSR Health, Inc. (NASDAQ:OSRH), formerly OSR Holdings, is a global healthcare holding company with operations in Korea and Switzerland. The Company has four wholly owned subsidiaries developing oral immunotherapies for the treatment of cancer and biologics for age-related and other degenerative diseases, as well as a diabetes-focused medical device developer advancing non-invasive glucose monitoring technology. OSRH also distributes medical devices and systems and is expanding into 4th party logistics (4PL). title: Beyond the Vendor Perimeter: Strategic Pentest for Third-Party Supply Chain Attacks
body_text: As reliance on third-party SaaS and PaaS solutions grows, vendor software has become a critical, yet vulnerable, extension of the corporate perimeter. Moving beyond passive risk assessments, we advocate for a ‘Shift-Left’ approach to third-party security. Through real-world offensive case studies, we demonstrate how to uncover and chain vulnerabilities before they compromise your systems. We offer actionable methodologies for supply chain pentesting, addressing the ‘Fourth-Party Blind Spot’ to establish a framework that fortifies your security posture against modern supply chain attacks. By Rajyavardhan Handa and Bhavin Makwana Every time your team integrates a third-party SaaS tool, you aren’t just adding functionality but you are extending your security perimeter. In 2025, the industry learned this the hard way during the Salesloft Drift incident . Threat actors exploited vulnerabilities in a simple chatbot integration, stealing OAuth tokens to gain unauthorized access to Salesforce instances, resulting in massive data breaches and permanent brand damage. This event wasn’t an anomaly; it was a wake-up call, proving that in today’s interconnected ecosystem, your enterprise security is only as strong as your weakest vendor. As organizations increasingly rely on third-party software, the attack surface expands. According to MITRE ATT&CK, adversaries may gain access to centralized software suites to execute commands and move laterally. This is compounded by modern development methodologies like microservices, containerization, and automated CI/CD pipelines, which, while efficient, introduce new layers of complexity. The Challenge: Beyond the Shared Responsibility Model While cloud providers offer a Shared Responsibility Model , the reality is often more complex, especially when SaaS and PaaS vendors abstract the internal engineering environment. The advent of Docker, Kubernetes, and Infrastructure as Code (IaC) has revolutionized how software is deployed. However, relying on vendor-provided images and automated updates introduces trust assumptions that may not align with your security requirements. Current automated scanning solutions often fail to mitigate these risks due to: Limited Visibility: Security solutions may have restricted visibility into the vendor’s internal processes and codebase, making it challenging to identify deeply embedded vulnerabilities. Delayed Updates: Vendors might release updates or patches at their own pace, potentially leaving customer environments exposed to known vulnerabilities until these updates are applied. Dependency Complexity: The complexity of dependencies in third-party products, such as nested libraries or hidden dependencies, can make it difficult to comprehensively scan and identify all potential risks. Evolving Threat Landscape: The rapid evolution of cyberattack techniques, especially those leveraging AI, can outpace the ability of existing security solutions to detect and respond to new threats effectively. Insufficient Integration: Security solutions may not fully integrate with all aspects of the vendor’s product, leading to gaps in monitoring and threat detection. Trust Assumptions: Relying on vendor-provided code assumes a level of trust in the vendor’s security practices, which may not always align with the stringent security requirements of the customer. Resource Constraints: Comprehensive monitoring and scanning require significant resources, and there may be limitations on the extent to which these solutions can be applied without impacting performance. By understanding these limitations, organizations can adopt additional measures, such as rigorous vendor risk assessments, continuous monitoring, and the implementation of complementary security controls. This includes effective penetration testing strategies to better manage the risks associated with third-party vendor products. Strategic Pentesting: The “Shift-Left” Approach To maintain a robust security posture, leading organizations employ a “Shift-left” security strategy. The core objective is to identify threat vectors and remediate risk before code goes live. This systemic approach is essential for any modern enterprise aiming to manage the complexities of the software supply chain, moving beyond passive review to active verification. In recent evaluations of high-volume data-managing SaaS products, Workday Offensive Security team moved beyond automated scanning which acts as a necessary baseline to deep, targeted security analysis. By demonstrating how vulnerabilities can be chained, we simulate realistic threat actor scenarios, from privilege escalation to server compromise. The Hunt: How We Dissected the Vulnerabilities To simulate a realistic threat, we didn’t start with administrative access. We requested a single, low-privilege user account within the SaaS vendor’s non-production environment. We treated this like a “black box” test: no inside knowledge, just the standard pentest playbook of information gathering, enumeration, and exploitation. What we found wasn’t just a single flaw; it was a path to total system compromise. The First Domino: The “Password Override” We started our hunt by looking at the vendor’s data lake product. As a low-privilege user, we were supposed to be limited to basic data access. However, while testing the database connection configurations, we intercepted the raw API request. Deep within the payload, we found a hidden attribute: “password override” It was a backdoor disguised as a configuration setting. By simply plugging in an administrative user ID, we could force a password change for that account without requiring the original password or multi-factor authentication. In a few seconds, we went from a “nobody” account to full administrative control. The result: We could kill the database connection, crash subsequent services, and, if we had the production host details, pivot directly into the production database. The Second Domino: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) While the account takeover was dangerous, the second vulnerability was more insidious. We noticed that the vendor’s new “workflow design” feature allowed users to build custom UI elements. It was an open door for malicious code. We inserted a simple JavaScript payload into the workflow fields. When an unsuspecting admin user accessed that dashboard, our script executed instantly. We weren’t just injecting text; we were effectively controlling their browser. We demonstrated the ability to: Steal session cookies: Allowing us to impersonate the admin user across multiple sessions. Remote Command Injection: Turning a browser-based UI bug into a remote server compromise. Automated Malware Deployment: Automatically triggering a download of malicious software on the admin’s machine the moment they loaded the dashboard. The Insight: The Fourth-Party Blind Spot Following our post-mortem with the vendor, the most shocking realization wasn’t just the vulnerability itself — it was the source. The flawed feature wasn’t built by the vendor; it was a defect in a third-party plugin they had acquired and integrated. This underscores a critical shift in modern enterprise risk: the “Fourth-Party Blind Spot”. We often vet our primary vendors with rigorous security questionnaires and compliance checks, yet we rarely have visibility into the sub-vendors, plugins, or libraries they integrate downstream. These tertiary dependencies inherit the exact same access permissions and trust boundaries as your primary vendor. In today’s interconnected SaaS ecosystem, you aren’t just vetting the product you bought; you are implicitly vetting every component the vendor has ever integrated. Securing your data now requires demanding deep visibility and contractual assurances not just for the vendor, but for the entire ecosystem they rely upon. Deep Dive: Cracking the Container Infrastructure Once we identified the fourth-party plugin risk, we turned our attention to the foundation: the containerized infrastructure itself. If third-party plugins are the hidden entry points, the Docker images are the vault. We needed to know: What are we actually running in our environment when we deploy this vendor’s product? We addressed this by reverse engineering the vendor-provisioned Docker images to peel back the layers of the application. This was not just a scan rather a forensic deep dive. What we uncovered exposed a dangerous gap between vendor claims and security reality: The Dependency Debt: We found that the third-party libraries bundled within the images were severely outdated. We weren’t just running vendor code; we were running legacy code that had been ignored for versions, leaving us exposed to known CVEs that the vendor had failed to patch. The “Hardcoded” Liability: Perhaps most alarming were the configuration leaks. The Docker images contained multiple instances of hardcoded credentials and were pre-configured to connect to internet-accessible database instances. It was the digital equivalent of leaving the keys to the vault in the lobby. The Container Compromise: By targeting specific vulnerable packages we discovered during the reverse engineering process, we were able to achieve remote code execution (RCE). From there, gaining root access to the containers was trivial. This forensic deep dive proved that our previous assumption — that the vendor’s CI/CD pipeline was “secure by default” — was fundamentally flawed. The automation that allowed for rapid deployments was, in this instance, simply automating the distribution of vulnerabilities. The Cascade: Chaining the Vulnerabilities We didn’t just find vulnerabilities; we proved they could be chained into a full-scale compromise. Because we had root access to the containers, the impact was no longer isolated but cascaded: The Container Breakout: We leveraged the vulnerable libraries to escalate our privileges to root user within the container, giving us shell access to the live environment. The Cloud Pivot: With that root access, we inherited the container’s cluster privileges in the Amazon EKS environment. This allowed us to pivot from a single container into various sensitive services across the AWS Cloud. The Persistence Vector: We identified a Kubernetes namespace specifically configured to pull updates directly from the vendor’s cloud infrastructure — a prime vector for an attacker to maintain persistence or distribute further malware. These findings taught us a crucial lesson: automated scans are a starting point, but they rarely capture the chain of risk. A library with a ‘low’ vulnerability, when combined with a ‘medium’ credential leak, becomes a ‘critical’ path to total cloud compromise. Conclusion The proliferation of third-party SaaS and PaaS integrations has fundamentally redefined our security perimeter. When these platforms include components that reside within your environment, their vulnerabilities effectively become your liabilities. We can no longer treat third-party security as a passive box-ticking exercise; it demands a “Shift-Left” mentality where continuous validation is the standard. If we don’t actively verify these integrations, we are effectively inviting the very risks we’ve explored like account takeovers, lateral movement, and cloud-wide compromise etc., into our most sensitive environments. True security today isn’t just about vetting your vendor; it’s about mastering your entire supply chain. Beyond the Vendor Perimeter: Strategic Pentest for Third-Party Supply Chain Attacks was originally published in Workday Technology Blog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: PartnerStack has a new Zapier integration!
summary: We’re excited to announce that we now integrate with Zapier!
body_text: We’re excited to announce that we now integrate with Zapier , the web automation app that allows you to integrate with the web applications you use regularly. PartnerStack already integrates natively with Stripe, SalesForce, ChargeBee and others - and our new Zap will make connecting to us even easier. Our PartnerStack Zapier App gives customers seamless integrations with Hubspot, Braintree, Paypal, MailChimp, Slack, and many other applications with our simple Zapier templates . This new integration lets our customers connect with different actions in PartnerStack automatically. They can trigger zaps when a new partner signs up, a new customer is created, a new lead or deal is created, a new reward or offer is generated, a new transaction is created, etc. For example, when new customers are created and pay, you can connect the ‘customer created’ trigger to a ‘create transaction’ action that creates a new transaction every time a new customer is added. Companies can use our Zapier templates to connect with their partners and integrate with other applications on and off Zapier - all the great things you used to do with our API but quicker and easier! Or you can always create a custom workflow with PartnerStack and Zapier. The new Zapier App even enables finding customers or partners and tracking events by sending PartnerStack data and events to your data warehouse. Give the new PartnerStack Zap a try and let us know what you think! ‍ Try the PartnerStack Zap PartnerStack Demo
